procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Judicature at Bombay
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the 23rd day of August 1954 of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay in Special Civil Application No. 1665 of 1954 under Article 226 of the Constitution of India.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant moved the High Court of Bombay under Article 226 of the Constitution for a writ of quo warranto or any other appropriate writ or order or direction against the 2nd and 3rd respondents, restraining them from usurping the office of the President and Vice-President respectively of the opponent No. 1 Municipality and restraining them from performing...
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court appeal was initiated by 'Special Leave' against the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals.

directions: The orders of the High Court are affirmed, though not for the same reasons.
The appeal fails and is dismissed with costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the meeting of the 3rd August, 1954 was invalidly held due to non-compliance with the notice requirements under section 35(3) and procedural requirements under section 19-A of the Act.

facts: A special meeting was called for July 30th, 1954, but was adjourned by the presiding officer, under instructions from the Collector, to August 3rd, 1954.
Notice for the August 3rd meeting was given orally to all councillors who were present at the July 30th meeting.
All councillors were present at both the July 30th and August 3rd meetings.
The notice for the August 3rd meeting was not in writing, nor was it posted publicly or published in a newspaper as specified in the Act.
The appellant argued that these failures to comply with the notice and procedural requirements of sections 35(3) and 19-A made the meeting invalid.
law: Section 35(3) requires three clear days' notice for a special meeting, which should be served on councillors, posted publicly, and published in a local newspaper.
The court interpreted the provisions of section 35(3) regarding the *manner* of serving the notice (in writing, posting, publishing) as "directory" and not "mandatory".
An irregularity in the service of a notice does not invalidate the proceedings unless it is shown that the irregularity prejudicially affected the outcome.
The presence of the public at a meeting is desirable but not obligatory, and their absence has no legal consequence on the validity of an election held at that meeting.
application: The court determined that the meeting was, in substance, held under the orders of the Collector, who had called the meeting and appointed the presiding officer, thus satisfying the procedural requirements.

Although the notice was not in writing or publicly posted, the court found that all councillors had received actual and "ample notice" of the meeting's time, place, and purpose, satisfying the core requirement of three clear days' notice.
The court treated the failures to provide a written notice and to publish it as "mere irregularities."
It was not alleged or proven that these irregularities had prejudicially affected the proceedings, especially since all councillors were present.
The court dismissed the argument that the lack of public notice was a fatal flaw, reasoning that the public's presence was not legally essential for the validity of the election.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the challenge, holding that the meeting of August 3rd, 1954, was valid. The court concluded that the meeting had, in substance, complied with the law. The procedural defects in the notice were deemed to be mere irregularities that were not mandatory and had not been shown to have prejudicially affected the proceedings.

issue.issue_text: Whether the election of the president and vice-president for the remaining period of the quadrennium was invalid for contravening section 19 of the Act.

facts: The president and vice-president were elected for "the remaining period of the quadrennium", which was a term of less than one year.
The appellant argued that this election was invalid because it contravened section 19 of the Act, which they claimed prohibited electing a president for a term of less than a year.
The High Court had previously dismissed this argument, holding that a proviso to section 19(1) allowed for such an election.
After the High Court's judgment and while the appeal was pending before the Supreme Court, the Bombay Legislature enacted a new law, Act LIV of 1954.
law: The respondents argued that the new amending Act (LIV of 1954) was retrospective and was specifically meant to validate all elections held during a certain period, including the one in question.
application: The Supreme Court found that the new amending Act (LIV of 1954) rendered the election valid.
Due to the passage of this new Act, the Court stated that it was no longer necessary for it to rule on the correctness of the High Court's original interpretation of section 19.
The new legislation effectively resolved the question of the election's validity, making the original challenge moot.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the challenge to the election's validity. It affirmed the High Court's order that the election was not illegal, but did so on the basis of the new amending Act (LIV of 1954) which validated the election, rather than for the reasons given by the High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the amending Act LIV of 1954, which validated the election, could be applied to pending litigation.

facts: After the election in question was challenged in court, the Bombay Legislature enacted Act LIV of 1954.
This amending Act was designed to be retrospective and stated that 'all elections to the office of the president or vice-president, held on or after the said date... shall be deemed to be valid'.
The appellant argued that the amendment should not apply to litigation that was already pending when the Act was passed, as it did not contain express words to that effect.
law: The Court established that the primary test is to examine the language of the amending statute to determine if the legislature intended it to affect pending proceedings.

Citing precedent (Mukerjee, Official Receiver v. Ramratan Kuer), the Court noted that if a statute is clearly retrospective, implying a 'saving' for pending litigation would render the statute's provisions 'largely nugatory' (ineffective).
application: The Court found no authority for the appellant's claim that an amending act must contain express words to apply to pending litigation.
It analyzed the language of the amending Act, specifically the phrase 'all elections... shall be deemed to be valid'.
The Court reasoned that if it were to create an exception for pending cases, the words 'all elections' could not be given their full effect, which would defeat the clear intention of the legislature.

Since the Act contained no saving clauses, either express or implied, the Court determined the legislature's intent was for the amendment to apply to all relevant elections, whether or not they were currently being challenged in court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the amending Act LIV of 1954 did apply to the pending litigation. The Court reasoned that the clear and retrospective language of the Act, which aimed to validate 'all elections' of a certain type, showed a legislative intent to affect all such cases, and creating an exception for pending proceedings would frustrate that intent.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the meeting of the 3rd August, 1954 was invalidly held due to non-compliance with the notice requirements under section 35(3) and procedural requirements under section 19-A of the Act.
appellant_arguments: The written notice required by section 35(3) was not served and published in the manner specified.

The requirements of section 19-A(1) and (2) were not complied with, as there was no evidence that the Collector had called the meeting or had made an order in writing authorizing the presiding authority.
respondent_arguments: All councillors were present on both 30th July and 3rd August, 1954, and therefore had ample notice of the meeting, its time, place, and the business to be transacted.
Any irregularity in the service of notice did not prejudicially affect the proceedings, and thus the resolution should not be deemed invalid.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the election of the president and vice-president for the remaining period of the quadrennium was invalid for contravening section 19 of the Act.
appellant_arguments: The election was invalid because it was conducted at the meeting of 3rd August, which was itself invalidly held.
There was an irregularity in the election with reference to the provisions of section 19 of the Act.
respondent_arguments: The election was valid because the meeting of 3rd August had been validly held and there was no illegality in the election.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the amending Act LIV of 1954, which validated the election, could be applied to pending litigation.
appellant_arguments: The amending Act is not retrospective to the extent of affecting pending proceedings.
respondent_arguments: The amendment is explicitly retrospective, as it is deemed to have come into force on a prior date (11th May 1954).
An enactment can take away vested rights of action in pending legal proceedings if clear language is used, and there is no principle that requires express words to do so.

statutes.act_name: Municipal Boroughs Act (Bombay Act XVIII of 1925)

cases.case_name: The King v. The General Commissioners of Income-tax for Southampton; Ex parte. W. M. Singer
cases.principle: An enactment does not require express words to take away vested rights of action for which legal proceedings have already commenced, but clear language is necessary to make the retrospective effect applicable to proceedings that were pending before the statute was passed.

cases.case_name: Mukerjee, Official Receiver v. Ramratan Kuer
cases.principle: If an amending act is passed during the pendency of an appeal and is clearly retrospective, it should be applied to the pending litigation, especially if implying a saving for pending proceedings would render the provisions of the statute largely nugatory.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A resolution passed by a municipality shall not be deemed invalid on account of any irregularity in the service of notice, provided that the proceedings were not prejudicially affected by such irregularity.
obiter: An enactment does not require express words to take away vested rights of action for which legal proceedings have already commenced, but clear language must be used to make the retrospective effect applicable to such proceedings.
It is not necessary to pronounce upon the merits of the controversy regarding whether a presiding officer has the power to adjourn a meeting.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Despite procedural irregularities in the service of notice for the meeting of 3rd August 1954, the meeting and the elections held therein were valid. This is because all councillors were present and had actual notice of the meeting's time, place, and purpose, and it was not alleged or proven that the proceedings were prejudicially affected by the irregularities. Furthermore, a legislative amendment can retrospectively apply to and validate actions in pending litigation, even without express words to that effect, as long as clear language is used to establish its retrospective nature.
legal_tests_applied: A resolution of a municipality shall not be deemed invalid on account of any irregularity in the service of notice upon any councillor, provided that the proceedings of the municipality were not prejudicially affected by such irregularity.

For a retrospective statute to be applicable to legal proceedings commenced before its passing, it is necessary that clear language should be used to create that effect, but there is no principle requiring that the enactment must contain express words to take away vested rights of action.
why_appellant_lost: The court found 'no substance' in the contention that the meeting was invalid due to non-compliance with the written notice requirements of section 35(3) and procedural requirements of section 19-A, because the facts showed no prejudice resulted.
The argument that the election was invalid because it was conducted at an invalid meeting failed as a consequence of the court's primary finding that the meeting itself was valid.

The court explicitly rejected the contention that an enactment can only take away vested rights of action in pending legal proceedings if there are express words to that effect, stating, 'There is no authority for this proposition, and I do not see why in principle it should be the law.'

The argument that the walk-out of 13 councillors rendered the meeting infructuous was dismissed, as their voluntary act did not invalidate the proceedings, and it was not suggested that a quorum was lost.
why_respondent_won: All councillors constituting the municipality were present on both 30th July and 3rd August 1954 and therefore 'had ample notice of the meeting to be held on the 3rd August, 1954, the time and place of the meeting and the business to be transacted.'

The appellant failed to allege or prove that the irregularities in the service of notice prejudicially affected the proceedings, which is the determinative factor for invalidating a resolution on such grounds.

The court's reasoning on retrospective legislation—that clear language is sufficient and express words are not needed to affect pending litigation—aligned with the respondent's position on the amending Act.
policy_considerations: The court prioritized substance over procedural form by holding that where all parties have actual notice and no prejudice occurs, a technical irregularity in serving that notice should not invalidate the proceedings.
The court rejected a rigid, formalistic rule requiring 'express words' for a statute to affect pending litigation, viewing such a rule as having no basis in legal principle.
